description:
Speaker: Tim Bakken, Professor of law in the Department of Law & Philosophy at the United States Military Academy

Abstract: Interpreted by the courts as a constitutional right, academic freedom, in theory, permits college teachers to express their expert opinions so that student will receive an education that is based on a search for truth, free from influences that would otherwise limit the search. This lecture concerns what happens when colleges, formally or informally, inhibit professors from expressing their opinions in class. Sometimes, the inhibitors in this academic environment are often fellow professors, as well as individual professors who censure themselves. The lecture explores how even tenured professors and advanced students may not perceive the many variables that lead to constraints on their communication and argumentation. Learning can become suboptimal, and the consequences can be long-lasting.

Short Bio: Bakken has worked in civil and criminal litigation in New York City, at law firms, and as an assistant district attorney in Brooklyn. He has been a visiting scholar or fellow at the University of Cambridge Faculty of Law, University of Sydney Law School, Columbia University School of Law, New York Law School, and Australian National University College of Law. 

He was an advisor to the National Military Academy of Afghanistan in Kabul, where he created the Department of Law. He has been a visiting professor at Ural State Law University in Yekaterinburg, Russia, and the University of Chile in Santiago as a Fulbright Specialist.

Join the lecture via ZOOM.

Please submit interpreting requests to myAccess.rit.edu.
title: Measuring the Value of Academic Freedom in the Classroom: How Professors’ Opinions Affect Students’ Learning and Performance, an Ezra Hale Lecture Series

description:
"Unboxed: the topography of Josh Owen" is an exhibition of instructional, utilitarian objects that define an evolving and active archive of designer, educator, and author Josh Owen’s work and observations.

Opening reception
6-9 p.m. Friday, Sept. 4
RIT City Art Space (32 Adventure Pl. Rochester, N.Y. 14607)
Free // All are welcome
A First Friday bus is providing FREE transportation for the RIT community

Using excavation as its central metaphor, the exhibition unfolds like a topographical landscape. The inaugural edition, JO.55, presents the initial 55 modular plywood boxes arranged on the gallery floor. These boxes function as both display units and transportable crates, allowing the exhibition to adapt to various spaces, emphasizing the dynamic and evolving nature of Josh’s work.

The exhibition is divided into three sections by color-coded trays: Professional (white), Pedagogical (black), and Phenomenological (red). Rather than isolating individual works on the walls, the exhibition presents them together in a cohesive, immersive display, offering viewers a collective experience that integrates Josh’s creative history. The installation celebrates how life and work are inextricably linked and how design can be a lens through which we explore both the material and emotional worlds. _RZLBD

About the artist

Josh Owen is the Vignelli Distinguished Professor of Design and the director of the Vignelli Center for Design Studies at RIT. Prior to his current role, Owen was director of the industrial design BFA program, in which he continues to teach his popular course known as the Metaproject. Owen is also the president of his eponymous design studio, Josh Owen LLC. His professional projects are produced by major manufacturers and have won many awards. Owen’s work is included in the permanent design collections of the Centre Georges Pompidou (FR), the Chicago Athenaeum (US), the Corning Museum of Glass (US), the Denver Art Museum (US), the Design Museum Brussels (BE), the Museum of American Jewish History (US), the Musee des beaux-arts de Montreal (CA), the Philadelphia Museum of Art (US) the Red Dot Design Museum (DE), and the Taiwan Design Museum (TP). Owen’s professional work has been featured in major exhibitions, numerous books on design, and is regularly included in critical design discourse. He is the author of the book, Lenses for Design.

Owen was born in the United States in 1970. Owen holds a BFA in sculpture and a BA in visual studies from Cornell University and an MFA in furniture design from Rhode Island School of Design. He has also studied at Tel Aviv University and Cornell University’s program in Rome. Owen’s studio practice is located where he lives in a small village a few miles down the Erie Canal from RIT.

Move from AI experimentation to strategic solution design in this hands-on build studio. Leave with a custom assistant in ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, or a similar platform—tested, working, and ready to refine.

Out-of-the-box AI can be impressive, but it does not know your team’s language, source materials, standards, decision points, or what good work looks like. In this hands-on build studio, you will turn that internal know-how into a working assistant for a recurring workflow, use case, or priority task—creating a reusable tool that supports real business work. During the studio, you will build, test, and improve the assistant in real time to see how it performs against the work and related goals you brought to the workshop.

Open to both the RIT community and the public, individuals and teams are welcome to register. Organizations ready to move beyond AI experimentation can also partner with RIT Certified to deliver a customized build studio that helps teams create, test, and refine AI assistants using their own workflows, trusted materials, and organizational standards.

Before the workshop, you will share an assistant blueprint from Workshop 1 or connect with us to confirm your use case, goals, and approved materials. Our instructors review that preparation in advance so they can anticipate questions and provide focused guidance as you build. In a public session, you will apply the build process to your own use case with instructor support. Customized training creates more room to shape shared examples, activities, and assistant design around your organization’s approved materials, workflows, standards, and goals.

During the session, you will define the assistant’s job, context, trusted materials, instructions, examples, guardrails, and review steps. Then you will test it against representative scenarios, identify where it needs more direction, and refine it with instructor support. You will leave with a working assistant, a clearer understanding of what makes it reliable and useful, and a practical plan for testing and improving it in your role or team.
title: AI at Work: From Blueprint to Build Mode Workshop

The RIT Academic Affairs AI Leadership Sprint is the launch of a year-long initiative to understand the status of AI in teaching and curriculum at RIT and to develop cogent policy that is sensitive to the needs of our faculty and students and reflects the expectations of different academic disciplines and professions.

Rather than prescribing one institutional answer to AI, the Sprint will equip our academic leaders with shared foundations and adaptable tools so every program leader can feel empowered to support more informed conversations, meet faculty where they are -- from enthusiasm to caution -- and move toward thoughtful, values-driven, discipline-specific action.  This sprint is aimed at RIT Department leaders, with some additional selected invited participants. Beginning with the sprint, we will lead with intent on AI, focusing our efforts on mission and values alignment, stakeholder needs, ethics and co-created policy that reflects insights at multiple levels of academic affairs.

description:
Move from AI awareness to practical application. Bring a mission-centered workflow and build a practical AI assistant to support communication, coordination, reporting, and mission impact.

Nonprofit teams are being asked to do more with limited time, lean staffing, and growing expectations from funders, boards, partners, and communities. AI can help, but only when it is used with purpose, clear boundaries, and human review.

In this applied workshop, you will learn how AI tools behave, where they can support nonprofit work, and where human judgment, privacy, and organizational context remain essential. You will explore how training data, prediction, hallucinations, prompts, source materials, and review practices shape the quality of AI-supported work.

Open to both the RIT community and the public, individuals and nonprofit teams are welcome to register. Organizations interested in building AI capability across their organization can also partner with RIT Certified to deliver a customized version of this workshop tailored to their mission, workflows, and operating environment.

Unlike workshops that focus primarily on AI tools, this workshop is built around implementation. You'll bring a recurring workflow from your nonprofit and use it throughout the day to identify where AI can add value, establish appropriate guardrails, and create a practical starting point you can test, refine, and share with your team.

We start with your mission and your work. Bring a recurring task, process, workflow, or use case from your organization, then explore AI through that lens. You will identify where AI can create practical value, what information it needs, what should remain human-led, and how to shape a responsible approach that fits your organization’s goals, tools, and standards.

You will leave with a practical AI starting point shaped around your nonprofit workflow. Together, we will define the recurring work AI should support, the outcome it should help create, the trusted source materials and context it needs, the instructions and examples that guide it, the guardrails it must follow, and the review points that keep people in control.
title: AI for Nonprofits Workshop

description:
What does it really take to build a career in design? Design leaders from across different disciplines share the stories behind their careers – the mentors who guided them, the challenges they faced, the risks they took and the moments of luck that changed their direction. Learn about their personal experiences of recognizing opportunities, overcoming setbacks and how a passion for design can turn into a life in design.

The event — part of the Vignelli Center for Design Studies' Design Conversations Lecture Series — is scheduled for 5:30 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 17, in Wegmans Theater (MAGIC Spell Studios). It is titled "Be Original Americas — Support, Challenges & Luck: The Road to Success in a Career in Design"

Speakers 

Casey Baxter, Vice President & General Manager - HBF & HBF Textiles

Omar Nobil, Senior Vice President, Creative Director of Product Design, Brand Creative, Visual Merchandising - Design Within Reach / MillerKnoll

James Cull, Design Director and Principal of Rottet Studio New York

About Casey Baxter

Casey Baxter joined HBF and HBF Textiles as Vice President and General Manager in April 2021. Based in New York City, she brings more than 20 years of leadership experience across sales, marketing, product development, and brand strategy within the commercial interiors industry. Throughout her career, Casey has focused on building and growing premium, design-driven brands, holding leadership positions with industry leaders including USM Modular Furniture and Bernhardt Design.

Known for her ability to connect people, ideas, and opportunities, Casey has built a reputation as a collaborative leader who cultivates strong relationships across the architecture and design community, notably through industry organizations such as the International Interior Design Association (IIDA), Female Design Council, and Be Original Americas, where she serves on the Board of Directors.

At HBF, Casey has led strategic partnerships that elevate brand visibility and deepen engagement within the design community. Notable collaborations with JUNIPER and ABC Stone have created innovative products, cross-brand experiences, and meaningful opportunities for customer connection.

Passionate about authenticity and innovation, Casey champions original design and collaborative leadership, bringing together diverse perspectives to drive growth and advance the commercial interiors industry.

About Omar Nobil

Omar Nobil joined MillerKnoll in October 2022 as Creative Director for Design Within Reach. Omar leads product design, brand creative and visual merchandising for DWR, Herman Miller and Knoll. Since joining DWR he has led the creative for collaborations with Vitra, Nick Cave, Paul Smith, Tracee Ellis Ross, Willy Chavarria, Sandy Liang and Boutique Homes. In 2026, he was included in the Wallpaper Magazine’s list of 400 people shaping creative America.

Prior to Joining the brand Omar has worked across multiple design disciplines but primarily in fashion. He was Vice President of Women’s Design at Banana Republic where he led the transformation of the women’s division to a majority percentage of premium, sustainable fabrics. He launched multiple new businesses including an athleisure collection (BR Sport) and inclusive intimates (True Hues).

Omar led collaborations with multiple celebrities and established the brand’s working relationship with Harlem’s Fashion Row- an organization focused on spotlighting talent in BIPOC communities. He also initiated a Banana Republic sponsored design competition for students at California College of the Arts and was a guest juror for the senior thesis students for multiple years.

In 2021, he co-founded Unincorporated Associates, a multi-discipline design studio covering architecture, apparel and custom automotive design for high end residential real estate developments. The studio focused on utilizing state of the art, energy efficient technology.

About James Cull

James Cull is the Design Director and Principal of Rottet Studio New York. He leads a talented team of architects and designers who create functional, aspirational, and layered interiors for leading hospitality, residential, and retail clients around the world.

He is a hands-on director and moves seamlessly between all building scales and disciplines—from master-planning to bespoke furniture detailing—crafting compelling spaces that have a strong vision, and rigorous approach. James is passionate about establishing a compelling design narrative, and devising immersive sensory experiences that authentically embrace “a sense of place”.

Over his career, James has designed bespoke interiors for landmark luxury brands such as Four Seasons, Ritz Carlton, Belmond, Park Hyatt, Peninsula Hotels, Wynn Resorts, Viking Cruises, Canyon Ranch, Guerlain LVMH, Barney’s New York, Equinox, Citi Bank, Bernhardt, and the New York Stock Exchange. His projects have been featured on the covers of Interior Design, Hospitality Design, and Sleeper magazines; and has exhibited his furniture at ICFF New York, and the Salone di Mobile Milano.

James holds a Bachelor of Art degree in Art History from Boston University, and started his career in New York working at contemporary art galleries in Chelsea. One summer, a chance design course opened a new door, and led to a Master of Science in Interior Design from Pratt Institute. Prior to joining Rottet Studio in 2016, James was a senior designer at Yabu Pushelberg. In 2018, James was awarded Interior Design magazine’s “HiP Award for Designer of the Year” in the Rising Star category; and in 2021, Hospitality Design magazine honored James with the “Wave of the Future” award.
title: Vignelli Center Lecture: What Does it Really Take to Build a Career in Design?

description:
Speaker: Martin Peterson, Full Professor of Philosophyand Elisabeth Scurlock Chair in Human Values of Ethics in Artificial Intelligence. South Methodist University

Abstract: This talk is based on my personal experience as Chair of the Academic Freedom Council at Texas A&M University (2024-2026). The contemporary moral issue I discuss is the following: How should students and faculty respond to institutional censorship? I will use Texas A&M's decision to censor Plato as a case study and identify four possible responses: anticipatory obedience, civil disobedience, malicious compliance, and what I call dissenting compliance. Anticipatory obedience—conforming to perceived expectations before being explicitly required to do so—is morally problematic because it reinforces and extends censorship. Civil disobedience, while admirable in many political contexts, may be less justifiable in academia when its expected benefits are small compared to the substantial personal and professional risks. Malicious compliance avoids capitulation but depends on deliberately disruptive, bad-faith adherence to rules. I argue instead for dissenting compliance: complying with institutional policies while explicitly and publicly expressing principled disagreement with them. Ideally, undertaken with a light touch and sometimes humor, dissenting compliance can expose unreasonable constraints without sacrificing professionalism.

Short Bio: Martin Peterson joined SMU’s Department of Philosophy as Full Professor and Elisabeth Scurlock Chair in Human Values of Ethics in Artificial Intelligence in August 2026.

Peterson conducts research in AI ethics, ethics of technology, normative ethics, and decision theory. His work examines philosophical questions about emerging technologies, with particular emphasis on artificial intelligence and rational decision-making.

Before joining the Department of Philosophy at SMU, Peterson was the Sue G. and Harry E. Bovay Jr. Professor of the History and Ethics of Professional Engineering and Professor of Philosophy at Texas A&M University, where he served from 2014 to 2026. He previously held academic positions at Eindhoven University of Technology and the University of Cambridge.

Peterson is the author of several books, including Ethics for Engineers (Oxford University Press, 2nd ed. 2025), Ethics in the Gray Area (Cambridge University Press, 2023), The Ethics of Technology (Oxford University Press, 2017), The Dimensions of Consequentialism (Cambridge University Press, 2013), An Introduction to Decision Theory (Cambridge University Press, 2nd ed. 2017), and Non-Bayesian Decision Theory (Springer, 2008). He is also Editor of Cambridge Elements in Decision Theory and Philosophy.

He received his BA and MA from Stockholm University and his PhD in philosophy from KTH Royal Institute of Technology.

Join the lecture via ZOOM.

RIT Academic Affairs AI Leadership Sprint for Department Chairs & Leaders

The RIT Academic Affairs AI Leadership Sprint is the launch of a year-long initiative to understand the status of AI in teaching and curriculum at RIT and to develop cogent policy that is sensitive to the needs of our faculty and students and reflects the expectations of different academic disciplines and professions.

Rather than prescribing one institutional answer to AI, the Sprint will equip our academic leaders with shared foundations and adaptable tools so every program leader can feel empowered to support more informed conversations, meet faculty where they are -- from enthusiasm to caution -- and move toward thoughtful, values-driven, discipline-specific action.  This sprint is aimed at RIT Department leaders, with some additional selected invited participants. Beginning with the sprint, we will lead with intent on AI, focusing our efforts on mission and values alignment, stakeholder needs, ethics and co-created policy that reflects insights at multiple levels of academic affairs.

Department chairs: Please choose one of two options and register to attend. If you are not available to attend one of these options, please ask someone from your unit to attend in your place; it is expected that every department will have representation or as a last option recordings of the virtual sessions will be available for viewing.

AI Sprint Schedule- Pick one option and register to attend by Sept 14 for the Sept 18 session or by Sept 21 for the Sept 22-24 sessions.

Both cover the same three sessions.

Questions? Jenna Sadue (CTL): jcsctl@rit.edu or Jen Schneider (Fram Chair): jlwcem@rit.edu  or Chris Collison (AI Hub): cjcsha@rit.edu

description:
DATE: Tuesday, September 8, 2026, 5-6 PM

SPEAKER: Dr. Alex Nikolaev, Associate Professor and Director of the Social Optimization Laboratory at the Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering (University at Buffalo)

TITLE: Optimization and AI for Quasi-Experimental Causal Inference

IN PERSON: Simone Center 1600 Atrium

ABSTRACT: Scientists across numerous disciplines attempt to identify and document causal relationships. Those unable to design and implement randomized (control) experiments to collect experimental data must resort to observational studies. To make causal inferences outside the experimental realm, researchers attempt to post-process large observational data sets to mimic experimental data. Manipulating the collected data to resemble experimental data is a challenging problem. Research in this field has enjoyed over forty years of success, focusing primarily on regression-based propensity score estimation and matching of individual treated and untreated (control) units, toward estimating treatment effects. This talk overviews the ideas and research directions more recently brought to the field by optimization and AI, from balance-optimal subset selection to neural balancing representation methods, highlighting their rewards and challenges.

BIO: Dr. Alexander Nikolaev is an Associate Professor and Director of the Social Optimization Laboratory at the Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering at University at Buffalo (SUNY). His interests and expertise are in stochastic modeling, optimization-driven causal inference, social network analysis, and healthcare informatics. He was a (co-)recipient of INFORMS Impact Prize and multiple National Science Foundation Awards. His current research focuses on the development of quantitative models to support decision aids in healthcare.
title: IRES AI-PROWIL Keynote Talk

description:
Imaging Science Ph.D. Thesis Defense
Femtosecond Laser Figuring and Finishing Towards Direct Fabrication of Micro-Optics

Zoom Link here

Cyril Otieno
Imaging Science PhD Candidate
Rochester Institute of Technology

Abstract:
Micro-optics enables small form factors, high resolution, and advanced optical functionality. The conventional fabrication approaches rely on opto-mechanical and chemical multi-step processes. While effective, sequential processing can accumulate form errors and the use of chemicals raises environmental concerns. We establish a methodology and develop a process for direct fabrication of micro-optics using femtosecond laser figuring and finishing. The interaction mechanisms and impact of laser wavelength, pulse duration, and focusing conditions were investigated. The fabricated micro-optics, including convex microlenses, microlens arrays, and scattering optics for surrogate laser beacon objects, were demonstrated. These demonstrations establish femtosecond laser figuring and finishing as a direct, non-contact, precise, and environmentally sustainable solution for micro-optics fabrication.

Intended Audience:
Beginners, undergraduates, graduates. Those with interest in the topic.

To request an interpreter, please visit myaccess.rit.edu

description:
Imaging Science Seminar
From Pictures to Quantitative Imaging Biomarkers: Use of Medical Ultrasound in Fatty Liver Disease

Zoom Link here

David T. Fetzer, MD, FAIUM, FSAR, FSRU
Abdominal Radiologist
UT Southwestern Medical Center

Abstract:
Chronic liver disease and metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) are increasingly prevalent worldwide, creating a need for accurate, accessible, and reproducible methods to detect, characterize, stage, and monitor liver disease. Quantitative ultrasound (QUS) offers a promising approach by transforming ultrasound images into objective measurements of tissue properties. This lecture will explore the principles and clinical potential of quantitative ultrasound for the assessment of hepatic steatosis, with a focus on three key acoustic biomarkers: attenuation, backscatter, and speed of sound. The presentation will highlight how these quantitative measurements can provide information beyond conventional ultrasound appearance and may enable more objective assessment of liver fat, including the potential to characterize different patterns of hepatic steatosis. Particular emphasis will be placed on ongoing research to develop a tissue-mimicking, lipid-containing liver phantom designed to replicate the acoustic properties of fatty liver disease across different levels and patterns of steatosis. This experimental platform provides a controlled environment for evaluating and validating emerging ultrasound fat-quantification techniques, investigating sources of measurement variability, and exploring novel quantitative acoustic biomarkers.
By connecting ultrasound physics, phantom development, quantitative imaging, and clinical research, the lecture will illustrate how engineered tissue models can help bridge the gap between fundamental imaging science and patient care. Ultimately, these efforts aim to improve the accuracy, reproducibility, and clinical utility of ultrasound-based assessment of liver fat and contribute to more accessible tools for the diagnosis, staging, and longitudinal management of chronic liver disease.

Speaker Bio:
Dr. Fetzer is an abdominal radiologist at UT Southwestern Medical Center, specializing in ultrasound, with a particular interest in quantitative imaging and tissue characterization. Dr. Fetzer is Director of Ultrasound at the Clements University Hospital and Parkland Health and Hospital System. He is also the director of the CACTUS lab (the Collaborative for Advanced Clinical Techniques in UltraSound). His academic pursuits span the use of ultrasound and contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) in liver disease diagnosis and surveillance, kidney and liver mass characterization, and ultrasound-guided interventional procedures. Dr. Fetzer performs research in quantitative biomarkers of chronic liver disease such as for liver fat and fibrosis, and in advanced contrast ultrasound visualization and quantitative analysis. Dr. Fetzer is an active member in and fellow of the American Institute of Ultrasound in Medicine (AIUM), Society of Abdominal Radiology (SAR), and Society of Radiologists in Ultrasound (SRU), and is frequently asked to speak, review, and write on the topics of ultrasound, contrast-enhanced ultrasound, and quantitative imaging, particularly for chronic liver disease.

Intended Audience:
Beginners, undergraduates, graduates. Those with interest in the topic.

description:
Chemistry and Materials Science Seminar
Developing Sustainable Plastics

Dr. Matt Miri
Associate Professor of Chemistry
College of Science, RIT

Event Details:
Synthetic polymers, most of which are plastics, are ubiquitous. Annually, global production exceeds 500 million metric tons. However, the current linear approach of using mostly fossil fuel-based plastics and generating plastic waste causes massive environmental issues. Our research group aims to synthesize more sustainable polymers. First, we will discuss published work on renewable polymers, followed by examples of biodegradable polymers. Among chain-addition polymers we synthesized are antibacterial ethylene/eugenol copolymers. We also investigated several step-growth polymers, such as tetrapolyesters from biobased phenolic monomers, polyfuranoates with substituted diols, and polybutylene succinate and its analogs with larger dicarboxylates. We will also highlight some ongoing projects. Finally, we will preview upcoming seminar presentations.

Intended Audience:
All are Welcome!

To request an interpreter, please visit myaccess.rit.edu
title: Chemistry and Materials Science Seminar: Developing Sustainable Plastics

description:
Join Marvel Comics artist Adam Kubert for an evening about visual storytelling and the craft of comics art. The exhibit Joe Kubert and the Art of Yossel: April 19, 1943 is on display this fall in RIT’s Cary Graphic Arts Collection, and at this event, Adam Kubert will talk about his father’s legacy in comics art with special guests. The discussion will be moderated by Daniel Worden, RIT Professor of Art History.

A reception and comic book signing in Wallace Library will follow. Free and open to the public. Registration is required.

Born 100 years ago in 1926, Joe Kubert is one of the great artists in comics history, celebrated for his iconic drawings of Hawkman, Sgt. Rock, Tarzan, and Tor, founder of the Joe Kubert School of Cartoon and Graphic Art in 1976, and acclaimed for his graphic novels Fax From Sarajevo, Jew Gangster, and Yossel: April 19, 1943. RIT’s Cary Graphic Arts Collection and Kubert Comics Gallery hold a significant archive of Joe Kubert’s studio materials, correspondence, process work, and original art, some of which is featured in the exhibit alongside Joe Kubert’s original art pages for the graphic novel Yossel: April 19, 1943.

Adam Kubert is an American comic book artist and part of the famous Kubert family of comic book creators, including his father, Joe Kubert, and his brother, Andy Kubert. He studied at the Rochester Institute of Technology and later at The Kubert School, founded by his father, where he also served as an instructor throughout his career. Adam began his career in comics lettering at the age of 12 on various DC Comics titles. Over the span of decades, Adam has worked on hit titles such as: X-Men, Fantastic Four, The Incredible Hulk, Avengers, Spider-Man, Superman, Ghost Rider and almost all Marvel titles in some form.  He is best known for his iconic runs on Marvel's hit series Wolverine.
title: Joe Kubert and the Art of Yossel: April 19, 1943 – A Discussion with Adam Kubert & Special  Guests

description:
Move from AI experimentation to strategic solution design in this hands-on build studio. Leave with a custom assistant in ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, or a similar platform—tested, working, and ready to refine.

Out-of-the-box AI can be impressive, but it does not know your team’s language, source materials, standards, decision points, or what good work looks like. In this hands-on build studio, you will turn that internal know-how into a working assistant for a recurring workflow, use case, or priority task—creating a reusable tool that supports real business work. During the studio, you will build, test, and improve the assistant in real time to see how it performs against the work and related goals you brought to the workshop.

Before the workshop, you will share an assistant blueprint from Workshop 1 or connect with us to confirm your use case, goals, and approved materials. Our instructors review that preparation in advance so they can anticipate questions and provide focused guidance as you build. In a public session, you will apply the build process to your own use case with instructor support. Customized training creates more room to shape shared examples, activities, and assistant design around your organization’s approved materials, workflows, standards, and goals.

During the session, you will define the assistant’s job, context, trusted materials, instructions, examples, guardrails, and review steps. Then you will test it against representative scenarios, identify where it needs more direction, and refine it with instructor support. You will leave with a working assistant, a clearer understanding of what makes it reliable and useful, and a practical plan for testing and improving it in your role or team.
title: AI at Work: From Blueprint to Build Mode Workshop

RIT's Vignelli Center for Design Studies presents Emanuela Frattini Magnusson, founder and principal of EFM Design, for its Design Conversations Lecture Series. The event is scheduled for 5:30 p.m. Tuesday, Sept. 29, in Wegmans Theater (MAGIC Spell Studios).

About Emanuela Frattini Magnusson

Emanuela Frattini Magnusson is the founder and principal of EFM Design, an international, award-winning, multidisciplinary practice that spans architecture, interiors, product design, brand development, and graphics.

Notable architectural projects include the Aqua townhouse development project in Miami, retail concepts for Russell Athletic, offices and showrooms for Knoll International, various art galleries and studios, a Times Square Hotel and restaurant, as well as number of residential projects in the United States and Europe, including the renovation of a Frank Lloyd Wright House in Rye, N.Y.

She has worked as the creative director of Spinneybeck leather. From 2013-17, she was Global Head of Design at Bloomberg LP, overseeing the design of their spaces at the intersection of local culture and global brand. During her tenure she completed over 40 projects in Australia, Asia, Europe and the Americas.

Magnusson a is a board member of NYCxDesign, a not-for-profit that promotes New York as one of the world’s design centers, highlighting the role of design in both education and business. She serves on the nominating and the finance and strategy committees. She is the president of Gianfranco Frattini Studio, the archival institution she co-founded in 2020 that interacts with manufacturers and cultural institutions for re-editions and exhibitions of her father’s work. In this role she has curated and designed two exhibitions in Italy in 2023 and 2026, as well as co-produced the first catalogue raisonné of her father’s design work, a 400-plus page book published by Silvana Editoriale in April 2026.

Throughout her career, she has created award-winning, top-selling products for leading manufacturers, including her Propeller Tables for Knoll, and a collection of accessories sold exclusively through the Museum of Modern Art. Emanuela has also served as a visiting faculty member at Parsons School of Design and as guest critic at Yale University School of Architecture. Her architectural and design work has been widely published in the United States and Europe. With an MA in architecture from the Milan Politecnico, she also holds an MBA from New York University’s Stern School of Business and is LEED accredited.
title: Vignelli Center Lecture: Emanuela Frattini Magnusson

Move from AI experimentation to strategic solution design in this hands-on build studio. Leave with a custom assistant in ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, or a similar platform—tested, working, and ready to refine.

Out-of-the-box AI can be impressive, but it does not know your team’s language, source materials, standards, decision points, or what good work looks like. In this hands-on build studio, you will turn that internal know-how into a working assistant for a recurring workflow, use case, or priority task—creating a reusable tool that supports real business work. During the studio, you will build, test, and improve the assistant in real time to see how it performs against the work and related goals you brought to the workshop.

Before the workshop, you will share an assistant blueprint from Workshop 1 or connect with us to confirm your use case, goals, and approved materials. Our instructors review that preparation in advance so they can anticipate questions and provide focused guidance as you build. In a public session, you will apply the build process to your own use case with instructor support. Customized training creates more room to shape shared examples, activities, and assistant design around your organization’s approved materials, workflows, standards, and goals.

During the session, you will define the assistant’s job, context, trusted materials, instructions, examples, guardrails, and review steps. Then you will test it against representative scenarios, identify where it needs more direction, and refine it with instructor support. You will leave with a working assistant, a clearer understanding of what makes it reliable and useful, and a practical plan for testing and improving it in your role or team.
title: AI at Work: From Blueprint to Build Mode Workshop

description:
Imaging Science Ph.D. Thesis Defense
Towards Optimization of Imaging Spectrometer Specifications: A Comprehensive Assessment of a Complex Ecosystem

Zoom Link here

MANISHA DAS CHAITY
Imaging Science PhD Candidate
Rochester Institute of Technology

Abstract:
The Greater Cape Floristic Region (GCFR) is one of the world’s most biodiverse regions, yet its ecosystems face growing threats from habitat loss, invasive species, altered fire regimes, and climate change. Monitoring how biodiversity changes across this vast and highly diverse landscape is essential for conservation, but remains challenging with remote sensing because the signals captured by imaging systems are influenced by complex variation in plant species, structure, and biophysical properties across spatial and spectral scales. These challenges are particularly pronounced in the fynbos, a hyper-diverse ecosystem where hundreds of plant species interact with light in complex ways and where fire plays a central role in shaping ecosystem recovery.
This dissertation investigates how remote sensing can be used to better understand and monitor biodiversity and post-fire recovery in the fynbos. The research combines field measurements of plant traits, high-resolution unmanned aerial system (UAS) imagery, and physics-based radiative transfer modeling within the Digital Imaging and Remote Sensing Image Generation (DIRSIG) framework. It examines the ability of remote sensing to distinguish vegetation across post-fire ages, predict biodiversity, and capture the spectral and structural complexity of fynbos communities. Virtual fynbos environments are developed to investigate how species occupy spatial, structural, and spectral dimensions during post-fire recovery and to systematically evaluate how changes in spatial and spectral resolution affect our ability to detect biodiversity.

Intended Audience:
Beginners, undergraduates, graduates. Those with interest in the topic.

To request an interpreter, please visit myaccess.rit.edu
title: Imaging Science Thesis Defense: Towards Optimization of Imaging Spectrometer Specifications

description:
Math Modeling Seminar
Full-Waveform Inversion for Medical Ultrasound Imaging

Zoom Link here

Dr. Rehman Ali
Postdoctoral Fellow, Department of Imaging Sciences
University of Rochester

Abstract:
Ultrasound imaging is widely used in clinical practice due to its safety, accessibility, and low cost, yet it remains largely qualitative, relying on images of backscattered echoes rather than quantitative estimates of tissue properties. In this talk, I present a framework for quantitative ultrasound imaging that inverts the physics of wave propagation to reconstruct spatial maps of tissue mechanical properties from measured waveforms. I discuss how this perspective naturally leads to full-waveform inversion as a PDE-constrained optimization problem. I also present experimental results in transmission ultrasound that demonstrate MRI-like image quality in breast imaging, highlighting the potential for quantitative ultrasound to complement or reduce reliance on more expensive imaging modalities. Finally, I outline the extension of this framework to pulse-echo ultrasound, where limited-view and highly ill-posed imaging conditions motivate related wave-based inverse methods. I conclude by discussing emerging directions in physics-based modeling and inversion strategies for improving robustness and clinical applicability.

Speaker Bio:
Rehman Ali received the B.S. degree in Biomedical Engineering (2016) from the Georgia Institute of Technology (Atlanta, GA, USA) in 2016, M.S. in Computational & Mathematical Engineering (2020) and Ph.D. in Electrical Engineering (2022) at Stanford University (Palo Alto, CA, USA). His research interests include signal processing, inverse problems, and computational imaging techniques applied to medical ultrasound. He is currently an NIH K99/R00 Pathway to Independence awardee at the University of Rochester in the laboratory of Dr. Nebojsa Duric to develop waveform inversion reconstruction techniques for imaging acoustic tissue properties using ultrasound computed tomography.

Intended Audience:
Beginners, undergraduates, graduates. Those with interest in the topic.
title: Math Modeling Seminar: Full-Waveform Inversion for Medical Ultrasound Imaging

description:
Across sculpture, photography, performance, and public installation, Mary Mattingly builds environments that ask how people might share water, food, shelter, and energy amid climate catastrophe. She approaches nature as a field of interdependence, one that depends on the ongoing maintenance of its fragile commons. Her recent project, Floating Garden (a collaboration with RIT), repurposes a mid-century 30-by-80-foot industrial barge that traveled from Rochester to Medina on the Erie Canal in 2025.

Mattingly will deliver a free and open-to-all artist talk at 6 p.m. Wednesday, Sept. 16, in Liberal Arts Hall, room A205. The event is part of RIT's Anna Ballarian Visiting Artist Series.

Developed in collaboration with RIT students, local gardeners, volunteers, architects, and agricultural educators, Floating Garden models a temporary commons: a space for nourishment and gathering. It was created for the inaugural Medina Triennial, on view through Sept. 7, 2026, in Medina, N.Y. The vessel hosts edible and medicinal plants, sculptural elements, biochar based water filtration systems, and a shelter for programming.
title: Artist Talk: Floating Garden Creator Mary Mattingly

Our fifth annual Together RIT: A Day of Dialogue will be held on October 23, 2026 from 10:00 a.m.-4:30 p.m. This event is only for the RIT community. The theme will focus on politics, religion, and spirituality.

Throughout the United States of America’s history politics, organized religion, and non-Western spiritual practices have been discouraged from public conversation. Our own families tell us such intersecting topics are not appropriate for the dinner table. Yet, we know the reality is that many people would like to discuss these topics. The question is how, where, and when. 

Together RIT creates a space to ask questions, empathize, build solidarity, and give recognition to our unique experiences. The day is also an opportunity to highlight the positive contributions, joy and pride that come along with identifying with a particular religion, faith, or spirituality. It is a day to seek understanding of political divisions in order to discover what we also have in common.
title: Together RIT 2026

description:
Can we know the future? If so, what does it mean for a claim about the future to be true?

This salon examines how philosophy, forecasting, and public policy approach questions of uncertainty, prediction, and truth. The discussion explores the role of evidence, probability, and scientific reasoning in making credible claims about futures—from everyday forecasts to long-term policy decisions.

Speaker Perspectives:

  • John Capps argues that dismissing knowledge about the future undermines public trust in science and engineering, both of which rely on making credible claims about future outcomes. Drawing on American pragmatism and theories of truth, he explores how we can responsibly evaluate claims about futures while strengthening democratic decision-making. John Capps is a professor in RIT's Department of Philosophy whose research focuses on American philosophy, theories of truth and knowledge, and democratic institutions.
     
  • Eric Hittinger approaches the future through quantitative forecasting and decision analysis. Rather than asking whether a specific prediction is true, he considers whether forecasts appropriately represent uncertainty. Weather forecasts, energy modeling, and probabilistic prediction provide examples of how rigorous uncertainty can produce reliable knowledge about the future. Eric Hittinger is Professor of Public Policy and Director of the School of Public Affairs. His research focuses on techno-economic analysis of energy systems and climate policy.

What is the Futures Salon? Talks, workshops, collaborative experiments, and public discussion, the Futures Salon supports intellectual exchange across disciplines while cultivating new ways of understanding and intervening in the worlds that are possible, probable, and preferable.

Please submit interpreting requests to myAccess.rit.edu.
title: Futures Salon Series - The Truth and the Future

New Energy New York (NENY) is a comprehensive ecosystem of project initiatives that support the establishment of an American hub for battery innovation, manufacturing, and workforce development in upstate New York — all made possible by a coalition of academia, non-profit, government and industry partners.

The 2-day seminar includes scientific lectures on lithium ion battery materials, technology, and hands-on training on the best cell fabrication practices from both academic and industry experts. During the laboratory training, attendees will receive hands-on experience using the RIT Battery Development Center’s semi-automated coin/pouch/cylindrical cell production equipment. The corresponding lecture program gives insights into the latest battery materials, electrode processing, and pouch cell technology trends which includes the newest manufacturing equipment. Methods for formation cycles and cell aging will be discussed. Attendees will receive training on charge/discharge schedule design and battery data analysis and interpretation. To learn more, please visit our website.

Cost: Free*
(Limit of 35 participants)

*Attendees must be employed by a US based company, student at a US university, or US citizen and agree to provide NENY metrics that track the impact of the training.

Speaker: Alessandra Buccella, Ph.D.

Title: Unpacking LLM-mindedness

Short Bio: Alessandra Buccella is Assistant Professor in the Department of Philosophy at the University at Albany. Her main areas of expertise are the philosophy of mind and the philosophy of artificial intelligence. Her current research focuses on articulating the ethical and societal implications of AI technologies within a framework centered on the notion of human flourishing. She is also interested in exploring how Large Language Models ‘think’ and whether their internal structures and processes resemble or approximate human cognition in any significant ways.

Abstract: Do AI systems like ChatGPT or Claude (aka Large Language Models, or LLMs) have minds? Some philosophers think they might. According to these philosophers, LLMs’ internal information-processing structures bear some functional similarities with mental representations and, therefore, might be seen as having “intentionality” – a notion many consider the “mark” of anything mental or psychological. In this talk, I try to disentangle the question of LLM-mindedness itself from the specific assumptions those who are open to the possibility make regarding the very notion of intentionality. Once these assumptions have been properly made explicit, I shall argue that, depending on how one understands the notion of intentionality, the very question of whether LLMs have minds is either meaningless or calls for an answer that is, at best, philosophically uninteresting.

 

ASL-English interpreters have been requested. Light refreshments will be provided.
title: Unpacking LLM-mindedness, a Cognitive Science Speaker Series Presentation

About LOT-EK

LOT-EK is a studio working at the intersection of art and architecture. Its practice of upcycling is one of reimagining—it reclaims objects that our culture dismisses, finding beauty in the ordinary. LOT-EK’s projects span from art installations to housing, cultural spaces for communities and museums, retail and mobile buildings.

LOT-EK is a tight group of creatives, that brings its voices and heritages to a common project. Founding partners Ada Tolla and Giuseppe Lignano live and work in New York, grew up in Naples, Italy, have taught at Columbia University GSAPP since 2004, and have been practicing together since 1993.

LOT-EK’s awards include the United States Artists’ Booth Fellowship of Architecture & Design (2011), the Architecture League’s Emerging Voices Award (1999), and the New York AIA Honor Award (2011). Our work is included in MoMA’s collection, and our second monograph, LOT-EK O+O: Objects + Operations, was published by The Monacelli Press.

WE START WITH THE THINGS WE FIND, a feature-length documentary on our work, premiered in 2023. Directed by Thomas Piper, the film explores the design thinking behind how LOT-EK brings the shipping container to life, the studio’s vision, and the soulful, lifelong partnership of the people behind the work.
title: Vignelli Center Lecture: LOT-EK

description:
Speaker: Hwan Shim, Ph.D.

Title: From Auditory Cognitive Neuroscience to Open-Source EEG/Audio Wearables and Unified Algorithmic Frameworks

Short Bio: Hwan Shim, Ph.D., is an Assistant Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering Technology at the Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT) and Principal Investigator of the Music and Audio Cognition Lab (MACL, rit.edu/macl). He earned his Ph.D. in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science from Seoul National University (2008). Dr. Shim’s background spans academia and industry, with prior appointments at Samsung Electronics (Principal Engineer), Stanford University, the University of Iowa, and Dong-Ah Institute of Media and Arts.

Abstract: Understanding the neural mechanisms of selective attention to a target speaker in complex acoustic environments provides a basis for the development of neuro-steered hearing devices. Auditory cognitive neuroscience studies have demonstrated that selective attention modulates cortical responses to target and competing sounds, motivating auditory attention decoding (AAD) approaches that infer a listener’s attentional focus from EEG.

This talk reviews recent progress toward translating these findings from controlled laboratory experiments into practical, real-world systems. I will first introduce neural mechanisms of auditory selective attention and the evolution of AAD from linear stimulus–response models to deep-learning and semantic decoding approaches. I will then present our ongoing development of an open-source EEG/audio wearable integrating dry EEG electrodes, microphone arrays, embedded processing, and audio output, together with efforts to reduce the number of EEG channels required for reliable decoding. Finally, I will discuss unified preprocessing and algorithmic frameworks for combining heterogeneous EEG datasets and improving cross-dataset generalization. Together, these efforts illustrate a path toward multimodal, wearable, and adaptive auditory attention decoding systems capable of operating beyond the laboratory and ultimately supporting real-world neuro-steered hearing technologies.

title: From Auditory Cognitive Neuroscience to Open-Source EEG/Audio Wearables and Unified Algorithmic Frameworks, a Cognitive Science Speaker Series Presentation

description:
Math Modeling Seminar
Atmospheric transfer of kinetic energy across planetary-scale circulation and weather

Zoom Link here

Dr. Pejman Hadi Sichani
Postdoctoral Associate, Department of Mechanical Engineering
University of Rochester

Abstract:
Earth's atmosphere is a complex, multi-scale dynamical system that continuously exchanges energy across a broad range of spatial and temporal scales. Analyzing the nonlinear transfer of Kinetic Energy (KE) across scales is central to understanding and predicting atmospheric evolution. This nonlinear coupling is a primary factor limiting weather forecasts over long timescales. Traditionally, such analysis relied on spherical harmonics, which are inherently global and cannot provide local information connecting scales with circulation patterns geographically. To address this, we apply a coarse-graining scale-analysis framework, which enables us to create global geographic maps of the KE cascade at any scale for the first time. This is made possible by generalizing the definition of convolution to ensure that the filtering operator and spatial derivatives on the sphere commute. In addition to an upscale cascade, we find a significant downscale KE cascade at scales smaller than synoptic scales. In the troposphere, we find direct KE exchanges between the planetary-scale circulation and smaller scales, including mesoscale motions. The exchanges occur in latitudinal bands of alternating upscale and downscale KE transfer driven by the Hadley, Ferrel, and polar cells. The physics behind such transfer is not due to a classical turbulence cascade, but is due to the action of planetary-scale strain against anisotropic effective pressure arising from sub-planetary-scale motions. These findings offer a novel perspective for exploring the interplay between weather and climate.

Speaker Bio:
Pejman Hadi Sichani earned his Ph.D. in Mechanical Engineering from the Vienna University of Technology, Austria. His doctoral research used Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS) to study the interaction of thermal and solutal stratification with wall-bounded turbulence, exploring internal gravity waves, energetics, and irreversible mixing in stably stratified flows. In 2022, he joined the University of Rochester, NY, as a Postdoctoral Associate in the Department of Mechanical Engineering, where he investigates atmospheric flow dynamics using scale-by-scale analysis, with a focus on kinetic energy transfer across scales in the troposphere and stratosphere. His research interests include computational fluid dynamics, turbulence theory, environmental and geophysical fluid dynamics, and high-performance computing.

Intended Audience:
Beginners, undergraduates, graduates. Those with interest in the topic.
title: Math Modeling Seminar: Atmospheric transfer of kinetic energy across planetary-scale circulation and weather
